To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the histone methyltransferase Gq9a is required for both activation and repression of gene expression by the glucocorticoid receptor.

1) the G9a methyltransferase is a positive and a repressive transcriptional regulator; 2) G9a functions by acting as a molecular scaffold to recruit coactivators to its target genes; and 3) G9a co-activator function is independent of its histone methyltransferase activity.
G9a is a positive and negative transcriptional co-regulator of glucocorticoid receptor (GR)-target genes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the role of G9A in transcriptional regulation.
the role of the histone methyltransferase G-9a as a corepressor and a coactivator of gene transcription in the nucleus.
the molecular mechanisms that regulate gene expression by G protein-coupled receptors.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

G9a is a coactivator and corepressor for distinct sets of GR target genes and that G9a co-activator vs. co-repressor function depends on the regulatory environment and chromatic architecture of the target genes.

G9a can be recruited by the GR to its target genes and can act as a coactivating and corepressing factor depending on the chromatin environment and the presence or absence of its catalytic methyltransferase activity.
G9a is an important transcriptional coactivator that can be recruited to GR target genes to regulate the expression of specific subsets of genes.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
G9a acts as a transcriptional coactivator for GR-activated genes and a transcriptional corepressor for GR-repressed genes.
the methyltransferase G-9a functions as both a positive and negative regulator of transcription, depending on the context of the gene and the transcriptional environment.
G9a is recruited to GR target genes and acts as a molecular scaffold to facilitate recruitment of coactivator proteins to enhance transcriptional activity of GR.
The main takeaway from our work is that
G9a can act as a transcriptional coactivator and corepressor depending on the gene context.
the positive or the negative actions of G-9a are determined not by the intrinsic activity of G-9 a but by the regulatory environment at target gene loci.
we identified a new mechanism by which G9a functions to enhance gene activation by GR and that this function is independent of its catalytic methyltransferase activity.
